text: Welcome to AWS Data Science. You already know how to build a model with scikit-learn on your laptop. This course does the same work on Amazon Web Services, where data is bigger, compute is rented by the hour, and a teammate must be able to reproduce your result. We start with Amazon S3, seen through a data scientist's eyes.

If you took the AWS Data Engineer path, you know what buckets and keys are, so we will skip that. What matters here is that S3 is the hub of an ML project. Raw data lands there. Processed training splits sit there. SageMaker reads training data from S3 and writes the finished model back to it.
Give every stage its own prefix. Keep raw data read-only. Put a version number in the processed path, so a new feature set never silently replaces the one an older model was trained on.

Now the file format. CSV is plain text, and you must read whole rows. Parquet is compressed and columnar, keeps data types, and lets you read only some columns. I saved a synthetic table of fifty thousand customers both ways. The CSV was about two million bytes. The Parquet file was roughly thirty-one percent of that.

In Python, boto3 is the general AWS SDK, and the AWS SDK for pandas, imported as awswrangler, adds pandas-style helpers. This snippet reads two columns from the training prefix. It is illustrative and not run here, because it needs an AWS account. Credentials should come from an IAM role, never typed into a notebook.

Finally, reproducibility. Fix your split once with a random seed and write it to fixed prefixes. I ran a stratified seventy, fifteen, fifteen split, and the churn rate held at about nineteen percent in all three parts. Then turn on S3 Versioning, which is off by default, so an overwrite creates a new version. Each version is billed as a full object.
You now have a clean home for your data. Next, the Glue Data Catalog turns those S3 files into named tables.
